passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel cognitive training program on working memory performance in adults aged 20–35. Twenty-eight participants were randomly assigned to either the training group (n = 14) or a control group (n = 14) that engaged in non‑cognitive activities. Over four weeks, participants completed daily sessions of 30 minutes. Working memory was assessed before and after the intervention using the n‑back task, recording reaction times (RT) and accuracy. The training group showed a significant reduction in mean RT from 650 ms to 530 ms (p < 0.01), whereas the control group’s RT changed from 655 ms to 650 ms (p = 0.78). Accuracy improved modestly in both groups, with the training group’s mean accuracy rising from 78 % to 85 % and the control group from 77 % to 79 %. The authors concluded that the training program enhances processing speed but has limited impact on accuracy.

Training (pre) | 14 | 650 | 45

Control (pre) | 14 | 655 | 50
Control (post) | 14 | 650 | 48
stem: Which of the following best describes the study’s experimental design?

options.A: Observational cohort study comparing two naturally occurring groups
options.B: Randomized controlled trial with pre‑post assessment
options.C: Cross‑sectional survey of working memory performance
options.D: Case‑control study matching participants on age and gender

explanation: Participants were randomly assigned to training or control groups and both groups were assessed before and after the intervention, fitting a randomized controlled trial with pre‑post measures.
trap: Option A suggests no randomization, which is incorrect.

stem: If the researchers had included a third group that performed a different cognitive task, what would be the most appropriate justification for adding this group?

options.A: To increase the overall sample size for greater statistical power
options.B: To control for the effect of any cognitive activity on working memory
options.C: To test the hypothesis that all cognitive tasks improve working memory equally
options.D: To provide a placebo group that receives no intervention

explanation: Adding a third group that engages in a different cognitive task would allow the researchers to determine whether improvements are specific to the training program or due to general cognitive engagement.
trap: Option D incorrectly describes a placebo group, which would receive no intervention.

stem: What is the approximate percent decrease in mean reaction time for the training group?
trap: Mixing up measures: the 7-point accuracy gain is not the reaction-time change; the RT fall is 120 ms relative to the 650 ms pre-test mean.

stem: Which statement is a misinterpretation of the study's design or findings?

options.A: Because the control group also repeated the n-back task and barely changed, simple practice is an unlikely sole explanation for the training group's speed gain.
options.B: The control group's mean RT changed by only 5 ms (655 to 650).
options.C: With 14 per group, the groups could differ by chance on unmeasured characteristics.
options.D: Randomization guarantees that the groups have no confounding differences.

explanation: Correct: D) Randomization balances confounders only on average; with 14 per group, chance differences remain possible. Why the others are wrong: A) The control group repeated the task and showed almost no change. B) 655 - 650 = 5 ms. C) Small randomized groups can differ by chance.
trap: Believing randomization guarantees identical groups, when it only balances confounders on average and small groups can differ by chance.

stem: Using post-intervention RT (training 530 ms, SD 38; control 650 ms, SD 48; equal n), what is the approximate effect size (Cohen's d) for the group difference?
explanation: Pooled SD = sqrt[(38² + 48²)/2] = 43.3 ms. d = (650 - 530) / 43.3 = 2.77, about 2.8 (a very large effect).
trap: Dividing by one group's SD or by the sum of the SDs gives different values.
